question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The consultants spent two days preparing slides and demos, but in the end their presentation to the board turned out to be nothing more than a ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A dog and pony show.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "A dog and pony show" means an overly elaborate or showy presentation that lacks real substance, often used to impress rather than inform. (एक दिखावटी और तड़क-भड़क वाला प्रदर्शन जिसमें असली सार कम होता है)
◦ Example: The product launch felt like a dog and pony show, full of lights and music but with very little real information.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The consultants spent two days preparing slides and demos, but in the end their presentation to the board turned out to be nothing more than a dog and pony show. This fits because the sentence criticizes a presentation for being showy but empty of real value.

 

• The expression comes from old travelling circus acts in which dogs and ponies performed simple tricks to entertain crowds, later used to mock any showy but insubstantial display.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "A cat and pony show", "A dog and donkey show" and "A fox and hound show" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing one of the animals in the original phrase with another, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Add fuel to the fire – To make a bad situation even worse (आग में घी डालना)

2. All ears – Listening very attentively (पूरा ध्यान देकर सुनना)

3. At the drop of a hat – Without any hesitation, instantly (बिना देर किए, तुरंत)

4. Back to the drawing board – To start planning something again from the beginning (नए सिरे से शुरुआत करना)

5. Bark up the wrong tree – To pursue a mistaken course of action (गलत दिशा में प्रयास करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Be waiting in the wings.
option_1: To hesitate and avoid making a decision for a long time.
option_2: To feel extremely nervous just before performing in front of an audience.
option_3: To be ready and available to step in and take over a role or task when needed.
option_4: To leave a place quickly and quietly without being noticed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To be ready and available to step in and take over a role or task when needed..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Be waiting in the wings" means to be ready and available to step in and take over a role, task, or position when needed, much like an understudy standing by. (पर्दे के पीछे तैयार खड़ा रहना, ज़रूरत पड़ने पर काम संभालने के लिए)
◦ Example: The vice-captain was waiting in the wings, ready to lead the team the moment the captain got injured.

 

• The phrase comes from theatre, where the wings are the hidden areas at the sides of a stage where actors wait before their entrance — so the idiom always implies readiness rather than nervousness or hesitation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes hesitation or indecision, which is the opposite of the readiness that this idiom actually conveys.

 

• Option 2 confuses the theatrical origin of the phrase (the stage wings) with stage fright, but the idiom is about being prepared, not about being nervous.

 

• Option 4 takes the word "wings" too literally, as if it referred to flying or leaving unnoticed, which is not what the idiom means.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Beat around the bush – To avoid talking directly about the main topic (इधर-उधर की बातें करना)

2. Behind closed doors – Privately, away from public view (गुप्त रूप से)

3. Bite the bullet – To face a difficult or painful situation bravely (मुश्किल हालात का डटकर सामना करना)

4. Bite the dust – To fail or be defeated (असफल होना)

5. Break the ice – To ease tension by starting a conversation (बातचीत की शुरुआत कर माहौल हल्का करना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

Someone or something that appears harmless or friendly on the outside but is actually dangerous or has bad intentions.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Wolf in sheep's clothing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Wolf in sheep's clothing" means someone or something that looks harmless but is actually dangerous or deceitful.
◦ (भेड़ की खाल में भेड़िया, यानी दिखने में हानिरहित पर असल में खतरनाक)

• This idiom is a classic exam idiom and is commonly used to warn people about hidden bad intentions behind a friendly appearance. (किसी के दिखावटी अच्छे व्यवहार के पीछे छिपे बुरे इरादे की चेतावनी देने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Wolf in sheep's clothing.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: A dark horse (छिपी हुई प्रतिभा वाला व्यक्ति): a person whose talents or intentions are unknown and who surprises everyone with unexpected success.
◦ Example: Nobody expected the new employee to win the award, but she turned out to be a real dark horse.

• Option 2: A fish out of water (अनजान माहौल में असहज व्यक्ति): someone who feels uncomfortable or out of place in an unfamiliar situation.
◦ Example: At the formal dinner, the young intern felt like a fish out of water.

• Option 3: A lone wolf (अकेले काम करने वाला व्यक्ति): a person who prefers to work or spend time alone rather than with others.
◦ Example: He has always been a lone wolf, preferring to solve problems without any team's help.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Burn the midnight oil – To work or study late into the night (देर रात तक मेहनत करना)

2. By the skin of one's teeth – Very narrowly, just barely (बाल-बाल बचना)

3. Call it a day – To stop working for the time being (काम को यहीं रोक देना)

4. Cost an arm and a leg – To be very expensive (बहुत महंगा होना)

5. Cry over spilt milk – To worry uselessly about something that cannot be undone (बीती बात पर पछताना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Once the merger papers were signed and announced publicly, the two companies knew they would ______, with absolutely no way to undo the deal.
option_1: Be past the point of no return
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Be past the point of no return.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Be past the point of no return" means to have gone so far in a course of action that it is no longer possible to stop or reverse it, whether the outcome turns out good or bad. (एक ऐसे मोड़ को पार कर जाना जहाँ से वापस लौटना संभव न हो)
◦ Example: After investing his entire savings in the new business, he was past the point of no return.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Once the merger papers were signed and announced publicly, the two companies knew they would be past the point of no return, with absolutely no way to undo the deal. This fits because the sentence describes a decision that could no longer be undone.

 

• The expression is believed to come from aviation, where the "point of no return" is the moment in a flight after which a plane no longer has enough fuel to turn back to its starting airport.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "On thin ice" (in a risky or precarious situation), "Back to square one" (having to start over from the very beginning) and "Up in the air" (still undecided or uncertain) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of an irreversible decision required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Cut corners – To do something in the cheapest or easiest way, often sacrificing quality (काम में कोताही बरतना)

2. Down to earth – Practical, sensible, and unpretentious (सरल और व्यावहारिक स्वभाव का)

3. Draw a blank – To fail to get any response or find any information (कुछ हासिल न होना)

4. Eat humble pie – To admit one's mistake and apologise (अपनी गलती मानकर माफी मांगना)

5. Fish out of water – Uncomfortable in an unfamiliar situation (अनजान माहौल में असहज महसूस करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Upset the apple cart.
option_1: To work extremely hard to achieve a difficult goal.
option_2: To disrupt or ruin a plan or situation that was previously going well.
option_3: To accidentally knock over or damage something physical.
option_4: To apologize sincerely after making a mistake.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To disrupt or ruin a plan or situation that was previously going well..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Upset the apple cart" means to spoil or disrupt a plan or situation that was going smoothly, often by doing or saying something careless. (किसी अच्छी-भली चल रही योजना या स्थिति को बिगाड़ देना)
◦ Example: Everything was arranged for the surprise party until her careless comment upset the apple cart.

 

• The key sense lies in the word upset, which here means "to overturn" rather than "to make someone sad" — the idiom pictures a cart of apples being tipped over, scattering everything into disorder.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes hard work toward a goal, which is unrelated to the idea of disrupting an existing arrangement.

 

• Option 3 takes the idiom literally, as though it were about physically knocking something over, rather than about spoiling a plan.

 

• Option 4 describes an apology, which has no connection to the disruptive action the idiom actually describes.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Get cold feet – To become nervous and lose confidence before doing something (हिम्मत हार जाना)

2. Get the ball rolling – To start an activity or process (काम की शुरुआत करना)

3. Give someone the cold shoulder – To deliberately ignore or be unfriendly to someone (जानबूझकर अनदेखा करना)

4. Go the extra mile – To make a greater effort than expected (अतिरिक्त प्रयास करना)

5. Hit the nail on the head – To describe exactly what is causing a situation (बिल्कुल सही बात कहना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To be excessively protective of someone, shielding them from every possible risk or difficulty.
option_4: Throw someone in at the deep end
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Wrap someone in cotton wool.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Wrap someone in cotton wool" means to be excessively protective of someone, shielding them from any possible harm or difficulty.
◦ (किसी को बहुत ज़्यादा हिफाज़त में रखना, हर मुश्किल से बचाना)

• This idiom is a classic exam idiom and is commonly used to criticize parents or guardians who are overly protective of children. (बच्चों या किसी की जरूरत से ज़्यादा हिफाजत करने के लिए इस्तेमाल होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Wrap someone in cotton wool.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Keep someone at arm's length (किसी से दूरी बनाए रखना): to avoid becoming too close or friendly with someone.
◦ Example: After being let down before, she preferred to keep new colleagues at arm's length.

• Option 2: Give someone a free rein (किसी को पूरी आज़ादी देना): to allow someone complete freedom to do as they wish, without restrictions.
◦ Example: The new manager gave her team a free rein to design the campaign their own way.

• Option 4: Throw someone in at the deep end (बिना तैयारी के मुश्किल काम में डाल देना): to make someone begin a difficult task without preparation or support.
◦ Example: On his very first day, they threw him in at the deep end by putting him in charge of the client meeting.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Hit the sack – To go to bed (सोने चले जाना)

2. In hot water – In serious trouble (मुसीबत में)

3. In the same boat – Facing the same difficult situation as someone else (एक जैसी मुश्किल में)

4. Jump on the bandwagon – To join others in doing something currently popular (चलन में शामिल हो जाना)

5. Keep one's fingers crossed – To hope that something will happen as desired (शुभकामना करना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The race was so close that the champion managed to ______, beating the runner-up by a mere fraction of a second.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Win by a nose.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "win by a nose" means to win by a very small or narrow margin, just barely ahead of the competition. (बहुत मामूली अंतर से जीतना)
◦ Example: The champion won by a nose in the final lap, beating the challenger by less than a second.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The race was so close that the champion managed to win by a nose, beating the runner-up by a mere fraction of a second. This fits because the sentence emphasizes an extremely narrow margin of victory.

 

• The expression comes from horse racing, where judges sometimes decide the winner by which horse's nose crosses the finish line first.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Win by a tail", "Win by a hoof" and "Win by an ear" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing "nose" with another animal body part, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Kill two birds with one stone – To achieve two results with a single action (एक तीर से दो शिकार करना)

2. Let the cat out of the bag – To reveal a secret carelessly (राज़ खोल देना)

3. Once in a blue moon – Very rarely (कभी-कभार)

4. On thin ice – In a risky or precarious situation (जोखिम भरी स्थिति में)

5. Out of the blue – Suddenly and unexpectedly (अचानक)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Throw one a curveball.
option_1: To present someone with a sudden, unexpected situation or question that catches them off guard.
option_2: To physically throw an object at someone in anger.
option_3: To deliberately lose a game or competition on purpose.
option_4: To give someone clear and detailed instructions in advance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To present someone with a sudden, unexpected situation or question that catches them off guard..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Throw one a curveball" means to surprise someone with something sudden and unexpected, catching them off guard. (किसी को अचानक चौंका देने वाली मुश्किल स्थिति में डाल देना)
◦ Example: The interviewer threw her a curveball by asking a question that had nothing to do with the job description.

 

• The idiom is sometimes confused with "throw a match" (to deliberately lose a game), but a curveball is about surprise and difficulty, not about intentionally losing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the idiom literally, as if it described physically throwing something, rather than presenting an unexpected challenge.

 

• Option 3 confuses this idiom with "throw a match", which is about deliberately losing a game, a completely different meaning.

 

• Option 4 describes the opposite of the idiom's meaning, since giving clear advance instructions removes any element of surprise.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Pull someone's leg – To tease or joke with someone (मज़ाक उड़ाना)

2. Put all your eggs in one basket – To risk everything on a single plan (सब कुछ एक ही जगह दांव पर लगाना)

3. Raining cats and dogs – Raining very heavily (मूसलाधार बारिश होना)

4. Read between the lines – To understand a hidden or implied meaning (छिपे हुए अर्थ को समझना)

5. Rule of thumb – A general, practical guideline (सामान्य व्यावहारिक नियम)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To dance nimbly and gracefully, especially with light, fancy footwork.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Trip the light fantastic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Trip the light fantastic" means to dance nimbly and gracefully, especially with a light, fancy step.
◦ (फुर्ती और नज़ाकत से नाचना)

• This idiom is an old-fashioned, literary expression and is commonly used, often humorously, to describe going out dancing. (नाचने जाने के लिए हल्के-फुल्के या साहित्यिक अंदाज़ में इस्तेमाल होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Trip the light fantastic.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Paint the town red (जमकर मौज-मस्ती करना): to go out and enjoy oneself in a lively, exuberant way, often at night.
◦ Example: After the exam results, the friends went out to paint the town red.

• Option 3: Kick up one's heels (खुलकर मौज-मस्ती करना): to celebrate and have fun freely and energetically, not specifically through dance.
◦ Example: After months of hard work, the team finally kicked up their heels at the celebration party.

• Option 4: Foot the bill (बिल का भुगतान करना): to pay the cost of something, especially something expensive.
◦ Example: The company agreed to foot the bill for all the employees' travel expenses.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. See eye to eye – To agree completely with someone (पूरी तरह सहमत होना)

2. Speak of the devil – Said when a person appears just after being talked about (जिसका ज़िक्र हो और वही आ जाए)

3. Spill the beans – To reveal secret information (राज़ बता देना)

4. Steal someone's thunder – To take credit for another person's achievement (किसी की उपलब्धि का श्रेय खुद ले लेना)

5. Take something with a pinch of salt – To not fully believe something (किसी बात को पूरी तरह सच न मानना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Losing the championship after leading for most of the match was a ______ for the entire team.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Bitter pill to swallow.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Bitter pill to swallow" means something unpleasant or painful that must be accepted, even though it is hard to do so. (कड़वी सच्चाई या दुखद बात, जिसे मन मारकर स्वीकार करना पड़े)
◦ Example: Missing the promotion after years of hard work was a bitter pill to swallow.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Losing the championship after leading for most of the match was a bitter pill to swallow for the entire team. This fits because the sentence describes a painful outcome that had to be accepted.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "A blessing in disguise" (something that seems bad at first but turns out to be beneficial), "A storm in a teacup" (a great deal of fuss over something unimportant) and "A piece of cake" (something very easy to do) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of a painful, hard-to-accept setback required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. The ball is in your court – It is now your turn to make a decision (अब निर्णय लेने की बारी तुम्हारी है)

2. Throw in the towel – To give up on something (हार मान लेना)

3. Tie the knot – To get married (शादी करना)

4. Turn a blind eye – To deliberately ignore something wrong (जानबूझकर अनदेखा करना)

5. Under the weather – Feeling slightly unwell (थोड़ा अस्वस्थ महसूस करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

The sound of leather on willow.
option_1: The creaking noise made by old wooden furniture.
option_2: The sound of horses' hooves striking a wooden track.
option_3: A term used to describe someone speaking rudely to another person.
option_4: A poetic phrase used in cricket to describe the sound of the ball striking the bat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A poetic phrase used in cricket to describe the sound of the ball striking the bat..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "The sound of leather on willow" means the distinctive sound made when a cricket ball strikes the bat, evoking the pleasant atmosphere of a cricket match. (क्रिकेट में बल्ले पर गेंद लगने की आवाज़, मैच के सुहावने माहौल का प्रतीक)
◦ Example: On a lazy summer afternoon, nothing is more soothing than the sound of leather on willow drifting from the village green.

 

• The phrase gets its name from the materials traditionally used to make cricket equipment — the ball is covered in leather, and the bat is carved from willow wood.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 confuses the phrase with the creaking of old wooden furniture, which has nothing to do with cricket.

 

• Option 2 wrongly connects the phrase to horse racing, but "leather on willow" refers specifically to cricket equipment, not a racetrack.

 

• Option 3 invents an unrelated meaning about rude speech, which has no connection to the actual cricketing image the idiom evokes.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Up in the air – Not yet decided (अनिश्चित)

2. Water under the bridge – A past problem that is no longer worth worrying about (बीती बातें जो अब महत्वहीन हैं)

3. When pigs fly – Something that will never happen (कभी न होने वाली बात)

4. A penny for your thoughts – A way of asking what someone is thinking (तुम्हारे विचार जानने की इच्छा)

5. Actions speak louder than words – What a person does matters more than what they say (करनी, कथनी से बड़ी होती है)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

A feeling of envy or resentment felt towards someone because of their achievements, possessions, or advantages.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The green-eyed monster.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "The green-eyed monster" means jealousy, an intense feeling of envy directed at another person's success or possessions.
◦ (ईर्ष्या या डाह)

• This idiom is a classic literary expression, first popularised by Shakespeare and is commonly used to personify jealousy as a destructive force. (यह मुहावरा ईर्ष्या को एक विनाशकारी भावना के रूप में दर्शाने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The green-eyed monster.

 

Additional Information

• Option 2: Cold feet (घबराहट या हिम्मत खो देना): a sudden loss of nerve or confidence just before doing something important.
◦ Example: On the morning of his wedding, he got cold feet and almost called it off.

• Option 3: A bee in one's bonnet (किसी विचार को लेकर सनक सवार होना): to be preoccupied or obsessed with a particular idea.
◦ Example: She has had a bee in her bonnet about healthy eating ever since her checkup.

• Option 4: Butterflies in one's stomach (पेट में तितलियाँ उड़ना, बेचैनी): a fluttering, nervous feeling felt before a stressful or exciting event.
◦ Example: He had butterflies in his stomach just before his first interview.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A bad patch – A difficult or unlucky period (कठिन समय)

2. A bird's eye view – A general view from a high point, or a broad summary (सामान्य या ऊपर से दिया गया दृष्टिकोण)

3. A bolt from the blue – A sudden and unexpected event (अचानक झटका)

4. A close shave – A narrow escape from danger (बाल-बाल बचना)

5. A cock and bull story – An unbelievable, made-up story (गपोड़ी कहानी)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Before the video conference began, the project head wanted to ______ so that everyone would be on the same page.
option_3: See eye to eye with someone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Touch base with someone.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Touch base with someone" means to make brief contact with someone in order to give or receive an update, typically after a period of no communication. (किसी से संक्षिप्त संपर्क करके जानकारी लेना या देना)
◦ Example: The two old colleagues promised to touch base with each other once a month.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Before the video conference began, the project head wanted to touch base with someone so that everyone would be on the same page. This fits because the sentence is about getting a quick update before an important meeting.

 

• The expression comes from baseball, where a runner must physically touch each base to stay in the game — the idiom borrows this idea of periodically 'checking in' to stay connected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Get in someone's hair" (to annoy or irritate someone), "See eye to eye with someone" (to be in full agreement with someone) and "Keep tabs on someone" (to keep a close, often watchful eye on someone) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of briefly checking in for an update required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A far cry – Something very different from what is expected or compared (बहुत अलग या भिन्न)

2. A fish out of water – Feeling awkward in an unfamiliar situation (असहज और अनजान परिस्थिति में होना)

3. A hard nut to crack – A difficult problem or a person hard to understand (कठिन समस्या या व्यक्ति)

4. A leopard cannot change its spots – A person's basic nature never changes (स्वभाव कभी नहीं बदलता)

5. A method in madness – A hidden logic behind seemingly strange behaviour (पागलपन में भी एक तरीका होना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

There's no such thing as a free lunch.
option_1: Everything is available at no cost if you know the right people
option_2: It is unwise to eat a large meal before doing important work
option_3: Nothing is really free; there is always a hidden cost or price to pay for anything received
option_4: One should always be generous and share meals with others
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Nothing is really free; there is always a hidden cost or price to pay for anything received.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "There's no such thing as a free lunch" means nothing is truly free — every benefit received comes with a hidden cost, obligation, or price, even when it appears to cost nothing. (मुफ़्त का भोजन जैसी कोई चीज़ नहीं होती; हर चीज़ की कोई न कोई कीमत चुकानी पड़ती है)
◦ Example: The company offered a 'free' trial, but as the saying goes, there's no such thing as a free lunch — customers were auto-billed after a month.

 

• The phrase is often used in economics and business to remind people that apparently free offers usually involve some trade-off or cost that is not immediately obvious.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 wrongly assumes that things can genuinely be obtained free through connections, which contradicts the idiom's actual point that nothing is ever truly without cost.

 

• Option 2 is a literal misreading that connects the idiom only to the word 'lunch' and eating habits, ignoring its real meaning about hidden costs.

 

• Option 4 confuses the idiom with general advice about generosity or sharing, which is unrelated to its actual meaning about there being no truly free benefits.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A nine days' wonder – Something that excites people briefly but is soon forgotten (क्षणिक चर्चा का विषय)

2. A piece of cake – A task that is very easy to do (बहुत आसान काम)

3. A shot in the dark – A guess made without any real knowledge (अंधेरे में तीर चलाना)

4. A stitch in time saves nine – Timely action prevents a bigger problem later (समय पर किया गया काम बड़ी मुसीबत से बचाता है)

5. A storm in a teacup – A great fuss made over a very small matter (राई का पहाड़ बनाना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

Completely loyal and unwavering in one's beliefs, principles, or allegiance to a person, party, or cause.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. True-blue.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "True-blue" means loyal and steadfast, describing someone whose commitment or allegiance never wavers.
◦ (पूर्णतः वफादार और दृढ़)

• This idiom is a classic descriptor of unwavering loyalty and is commonly used for devoted supporters of a person, party, or cause. (यह मुहावरा किसी व्यक्ति, दल या उद्देश्य के प्रति अटूट निष्ठा दिखाने वाले व्यक्ति के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. True-blue.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Fair-weather friend (मतलबी दोस्त, जो सिर्फ अच्छे समय में साथ दे): someone who is only supportive and loyal when things are going well, but disappears in difficult times.
◦ Example: When he lost his job, he realized most of his friends were just fair-weather friends.

• Option 2: Turn over a new leaf (नई शुरुआत करना, सुधरना): to start behaving in a better or more responsible way than before.
◦ Example: After the accident, he decided to turn over a new leaf and quit smoking.

• Option 3: Sit on the fence (तटस्थ रहना, पक्ष न लेना): to avoid making a decision or taking sides in a dispute.
◦ Example: The politician preferred to sit on the fence rather than commit to either party's proposal.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A wet blanket – A person who spoils others' fun or enthusiasm (मज़ा किरकिरा करने वाला व्यक्ति)

2. Add fuel to the fire – To make a bad situation even worse (आग में घी डालना)

3. All ears – Listening eagerly and attentively (पूरा ध्यान से सुनना)

4. All thumbs – Clumsy or awkward with one's hands (अनाड़ी, फूहड़)

5. An axe to grind – To have a personal or selfish reason for doing something (स्वार्थ का उद्देश्य होना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The soldiers fought ______ to defend the fort till the last breath.
option_4: At the drop of a hat
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. With might and main.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "With might and main" means with all one's physical strength and power, i.e., using every ounce of energy and effort available. (पूरी ताकत और शक्ति के साथ)
◦ Example: He pushed the stalled car with might and main until it finally moved.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The soldiers fought with might and main to defend the fort till the last breath. This fits because the sentence describes an all-out physical effort in battle.

 

• The expression comes from Old English, where 'might' and 'main' were both separate words for physical strength and power, later joined together for emphasis.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "With a heavy heart" (feeling sad or reluctant while doing something), "By hook or by crook" (by any means necessary, fair or unfair) and "At the drop of a hat" (immediately, without any hesitation) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of using full physical strength required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Apple of one's eye – A person who is dearly loved above all others (आँखों का तारा)

2. At loggerheads – In strong disagreement or conflict with someone (कड़े मतभेद में होना)

3. Back to square one – Having to start something all over again (फिर से शुरुआत करनी पड़ना)

4. Bark up the wrong tree – To accuse or blame the wrong person (गलत व्यक्ति पर आरोप लगाना)

5. Beat around the bush – To avoid talking directly about the main point (घुमा-फिराकर बात करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

To be on last legs.
option_1: To be extremely tall or physically imposing
option_2: To be in a very weak or failing state, close to breaking down or ending completely
option_3: To be walking very slowly due to tiredness
option_4: To be standing firmly and confidently in one's position
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To be in a very weak or failing state, close to breaking down or ending completely.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "To be on last legs" means to be in a very weak, worn-out, or failing condition, close to breaking down or coming to an end, whether referring to a person, object, or institution. (अंतिम सांसें गिनना, टूटने के कगार पर होना)
◦ Example: The old washing machine is on its last legs and needs to be replaced soon.

 

• The phrase is commonly applied not just to people's health but also to failing businesses, old machines, and worn-out relationships nearing collapse.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 confuses the word 'legs' with physical height, but the idiom has nothing to do with a person's or object's stature.

 

• Option 3 is a literal misreading focused only on the act of walking, missing the idiom's real sense of being close to failure or collapse.

 

• Option 4 describes the opposite of the idiom's meaning — standing firm and confident — whereas the idiom actually signals weakness and imminent failure.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Bite the bullet – To face a difficult or painful situation with courage (साहस के साथ कठिनाई का सामना करना)

2. Blow one's own trumpet – To boast about one's own achievements (अपनी तारीफ खुद करना)

3. Break the ice – To ease tension or start a conversation in an awkward setting (बातचीत की शुरुआत करना)

4. Burn the midnight oil – To work or study late into the night (देर रात तक मेहनत करना)

5. By the skin of one's teeth – To narrowly succeed at something (बहुत मुश्किल से बच निकलना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

For a very long and indefinite period of time, with no clear end in sight.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Till the cows come home.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Till the cows come home" means for a very long, indefinite amount of time, often implying something could go on almost endlessly.
◦ (बहुत लंबे और अनिश्चित समय तक)

• This idiom is a rural, farm-based expression and is commonly used humorously to emphasize that an activity could continue indefinitely. (यह मुहावरा हास्यपूर्ण ढंग से किसी काम के अनिश्चित काल तक चलते रहने को दर्शाता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Till the cows come home.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Once in a blue moon (कभी-कभार, बहुत कम): something that happens very rarely.
◦ Example: He visits his hometown once in a blue moon these days.

• Option 2: In the nick of time (ऐन वक्त पर, आखिरी क्षण में): at the very last possible moment, just before it is too late.
◦ Example: The doctor arrived in the nick of time to save the patient.

• Option 4: At the eleventh hour (आखिरी समय पर): at the last possible moment before a deadline.
◦ Example: She finished the project at the eleventh hour, just before submission.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Call it a day – To stop doing something for the rest of the day (काम को वहीं समाप्त कर देना)

2. Cast pearls before swine – To offer something valuable to someone who cannot appreciate it (सुअर के आगे मोती डालना)

3. Cry over spilt milk – To regret something that has already happened and cannot be changed (बीती बात पर पछताना)

4. Cut corners – To do something in the cheapest or easiest way, sacrificing quality (काम में कोताही बरतना)

5. Cut to the chase – To get straight to the point without wasting time (सीधे मुद्दे पर आना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

She wished she could be a ______ during the board meeting to know what was really being discussed about the merger.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Fly on the wall.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Fly on the wall" means an unnoticed, silent observer who watches a situation without being seen or participating in it. (दीवार पर बैठी मक्खी, अर्थात एक गुप्त और अनदेखा दर्शक)
◦ Example: I would love to be a fly on the wall during their private negotiations.

 

• The completed sentence reads: She wished she could be a fly on the wall during the board meeting to know what was really being discussed about the merger. This fits because she wants to secretly observe the discussion without being noticed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "A dark horse" (a person whose abilities or intentions are little known, especially one who unexpectedly succeeds), "Wolf in sheep's clothing" (someone dangerous who pretends to be harmless) and "Lone wolf" (a person who prefers to act or work alone) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of secretly and silently observing a situation required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Devil's advocate – Someone who argues the opposite side of a debate to test it (जानबूझकर विरोधी पक्ष रखने वाला)

2. Down to earth – Practical, humble, and sensible in one's approach (सरल और व्यावहारिक स्वभाव)

3. Draw a blank – To fail to remember or find something (कुछ भी याद न आना)

4. Eat humble pie – To apologize humbly after being proven wrong (विनम्रता से माफी मांगना)

5. Face the music – To accept the unpleasant consequences of one's actions (परिणाम भुगतने के लिए तैयार होना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

With tongue in cheek.
option_1: Said or done in a joking, insincere manner while appearing to be serious
option_2: Spoken with great anger and frustration
option_3: Expressed with complete honesty and deep sincerity
option_4: Said very quietly so that no one else can hear
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Said or done in a joking, insincere manner while appearing to be serious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "With tongue in cheek" means said or done in a joking or ironic way while maintaining an outwardly serious expression, so the listener must sense the humour is not meant literally. (हल्के-फुल्के या व्यंग्यात्मक ढंग से, गंभीर दिखते हुए मजाक में कहना)
◦ Example: His review of the restaurant was written tongue in cheek, praising the terrible service as 'refreshingly honest'.

 

• The key to this idiom is that the speaker's words should not be taken literally — the real point is often the opposite of, or an exaggeration on, what is actually said.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 wrongly associates the idiom with anger, but the phrase actually conveys humour and irony, not frustration.

 

• Option 3 describes the opposite of the idiom's meaning — the idiom signals insincerity or playful exaggeration, not genuine sincerity.

 

• Option 4 confuses the idiom with a description of volume or secrecy, whereas it actually concerns tone and intent, not how loudly something is said.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Fair and square – Done honestly, according to the rules (पूरी ईमानदारी से)

2. Feather in one's cap – An achievement one can be proud of (गौरव की उपलब्धि)

3. Get the sack – To be dismissed or fired from a job (नौकरी से निकाल दिया जाना)

4. Give someone the benefit of the doubt – To trust what someone says without full proof (बिना पूरे सबूत के भरोसा करना)

5. Go the extra mile – To make an extra effort beyond what is expected (अपेक्षा से अधिक प्रयास करना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

A new, unfamiliar situation or area of experience involving unknown risks or challenges, where there is no precedent to rely on.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Uncharted waters.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Uncharted waters" means a new and unfamiliar situation with unknown risks, where no one has clear experience or guidance to draw upon.
◦ (अनजान और जोखिम भरी नई स्थिति)

• This idiom is a nautical metaphor and is commonly used for situations such as new technology, unfamiliar markets, or unprecedented circumstances. (यह मुहावरा नई और अनिश्चित परिस्थितियों के लिए प्रयोग किया जाता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Uncharted waters.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Smooth sailing (आसान और परेशानी रहित यात्रा/स्थिति): a situation that proceeds easily, without any difficulties.
◦ Example: Once the approvals came through, it was smooth sailing for the new project.

• Option 3: Par for the course (सामान्य या अपेक्षित बात): something that is typical or expected in a particular situation.
◦ Example: Long delays at this airport are just par for the course during the holiday season.

• Option 4: Water under the bridge (बीती बात, जो अब मायने नहीं रखती): past events or disagreements that are no longer important and should be forgotten.
◦ Example: We had our differences years ago, but that's all water under the bridge now.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Hit the nail on the head – To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem (सही बात कहना)

2. Hit the sack – To go to bed or go to sleep (सोने जाना)

3. In hot water – In a difficult or troublesome situation (मुसीबत में)

4. In the same boat – Facing the same difficult situation as someone else (एक जैसी मुश्किल स्थिति में)

5. Jump on the bandwagon – To join a popular activity or trend that others are already doing (लोकप्रिय प्रवृत्ति में शामिल हो जाना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The two neighbors argued loudly over a parking spot, but everyone agreed it was just ______ that would be forgotten by next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A tempest in a teapot.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "A tempest in a teapot" means a disproportionately strong or angry reaction to a matter that is actually quite trivial, i.e., making a big issue out of something small. (छोटी बात का बतंगड़ बनाना)
◦ Example: The office debate over the seating arrangement turned out to be a tempest in a teapot.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The two neighbors argued loudly over a parking spot, but everyone agreed it was just a tempest in a teapot that would be forgotten by next week. This fits because the dispute was minor despite the loud reaction it caused.

 

• The expression is a variation of the older British idiom 'a storm in a teacup', both using the image of a tiny teapot to mock an overblown reaction to a small matter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "A blessing in disguise" (something that seems bad at first but turns out to be beneficial), "A drop in the ocean" (an amount so small it makes almost no difference) and "A leap in the dark" (an action taken without knowing what the consequences will be) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of a trivial matter blown out of proportion required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Keep an eye on – To watch someone or something carefully (ध्यान से नज़र रखना)

2. Kill two birds with one stone – To achieve two things with a single action (एक तीर से दो शिकार करना)

3. Let the cat out of the bag – To accidentally reveal a secret (राज़ खोल देना)

4. Once in a blue moon – Something that happens very rarely (कभी-कभार)

5. On cloud nine – Extremely happy and joyful (बेहद खुश होना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Think on one's feet.
option_1: To stand for long hours without getting tired
option_2: To walk quickly from one place to another without stopping
option_3: To carefully plan every detail well in advance before acting
option_4: To think and react quickly and effectively in a stressful or unexpected situation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To think and react quickly and effectively in a stressful or unexpected situation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Think on one's feet" means to think clearly, quickly, and effectively when faced with an unexpected or stressful situation, coming up with a solution on the spot. (तुरंत और सूझबूझ से सोचकर हल निकालना)
◦ Example: A good debater must be able to think on her feet when the opponent raises an unexpected point.

 

• The idiom highlights speed and adaptability of thought under pressure — it is the opposite of relying on a pre-prepared plan, which is a common point of confusion for this idiom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 wrongly takes the idiom literally, connecting it to physical stamina or standing, which has nothing to do with its actual meaning about quick thinking.

 

• Option 2 is another literal misreading, focusing on the act of walking rather than the idiom's real sense of rapid mental response.

 

• Option 3 describes the opposite of the idiom's meaning — careful advance planning — whereas the idiom is specifically about improvising quickly without prior preparation.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Out of the blue – Something that happens suddenly and unexpectedly (अचानक, बिना किसी सूचना के)

2. Pull someone's leg – To playfully tease or joke with someone (किसी का मज़ाक उड़ाना)

3. Rain cats and dogs – To rain very heavily (मूसलाधार बारिश होना)

4. Read between the lines – To understand a hidden or implied meaning (छिपे हुए अर्थ को समझना)

5. Ring a bell – To sound familiar or remind one of something (परिचित लगना, याद दिलाना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

Lacking experience and being immature, especially because of youth or newness to a role.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wet behind the ears.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Wet behind the ears" means lacking experience; immature.
◦ (अनुभवहीन और अपरिपक्व)

• This idiom is informal and slightly mocking and is commonly used to describe newcomers who are new to a job or situation. (यह मुहावरा नए और अनुभवहीन व्यक्ति के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wet behind the ears.

 

Additional Information

• Option 2: Long in the tooth (बूढ़ा / उम्रदराज़): means someone who is quite old or aging.
◦ Example: He felt a bit long in the tooth to be starting a new career at sixty.

• Option 3: An old hand (अनुभवी व्यक्ति): means a person who is very experienced at something.
◦ Example: She's an old hand at organising conferences, having done it for twenty years.

• Option 4: Cut one's teeth (अनुभव प्राप्त करना): means to gain one's first experience of a particular type of work.
◦ Example: He cut his teeth as a journalist working for a small local newspaper.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A Bad Patch – A difficult period (कठिन समय)

2. A Blessing In Disguise – Something good that seemed bad at first (छिपा हुआ वरदान)

3. A Drop In The Ocean – A very small amount compared to what is needed (ऊंट के मुंह में जीरा)

4. A Piece Of Cake – Something very easy to do (बहुत आसान काम)

5. Add Fuel To The Fire – To make a bad situation even worse (आग में घी डालना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

She was warned never to ______ about what happened at the family meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tell tales out of school.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Tell tales out of school" means to reveal private, sensitive, or confidential information, especially something shared in trust. (व्यक्तिगत या गोपनीय जानकारी बाहर बता देना)
◦ Example: He was asked to keep the discussion confidential, but he ended up telling tales out of school to a reporter.

 

• The completed sentence reads: She was warned never to tell tales out of school about what happened at the family meeting. This fits because it warns her against leaking private family matters to outsiders.

 

• The expression comes from old English boarding schools, where pupils were expected not to report on classmates' private misbehaviour to teachers or outsiders; it later broadened to mean revealing any confidential matter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Tell tall tales" (to narrate exaggerated or made-up stories), "Beat about the bush" (to avoid speaking directly about the main point) and "Cry wolf" (to raise a false alarm) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of leaking confidential information required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. An Axe To Grind – A personal or selfish reason for doing something (स्वार्थ छिपा होना)

2. At The Drop Of A Hat – Immediately, without any hesitation (तुरंत, बिना देर किए)

3. Back To Square One – To start over again from the beginning (फिर से शुरुआत करना)

4. Barking Up The Wrong Tree – Pursuing a mistaken or misguided course of action (गलत दिशा में प्रयास करना)

5. Beat Around The Bush – To avoid talking directly about the main point (इधर-उधर की बातें करना)
